findings.title: createRecoveryCodesCredential stores raw recovery codes in user storage instead of hashed codes
findings.body: The new method createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated recovery codes (generatedCodes) to JSON and passes that JSON as the challengeResponse of a UserCredentialModel to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). For local (Keycloak DB) storage, the recoveryCodeCredentialProvider.createCredential(realm, user, credentialModel) path is used, and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes each raw code before persisting. But when the credential is stored in federated user storage, the raw, unhashed codes are handed to the storage provider verbatim. Any user storage provider that persists the credential data as-is (as the test provider BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage does at line 197 with recoveryCodesModel.setCredentialData(input.getChallengeResponse())) will store the recovery codes in plaintext. Recovery codes are bearer credentials equivalent to passwords; storing them unhashed in an external user storage is a serious data-integrity/security issue, and it also breaks the validation contract: the local RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider validates input by hashing the input and comparing to the stored hash, while a federated provider receiving raw codes must compare raw-to-raw (as the test provider does at line 340), meaning the same code validates differently depending on where it is stored. The fix is to hash the codes (e.g. via RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) before building the UserCredentialModel passed to updateCredential, and to construct the credential model consistently for both storage paths.

The credentialModel parameter (a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel) carries the generatedAt timestamp and userLabel, but these are not transferred to the UserCredentialModel — only type and challengeResponse (the JSON) are set. The id is empty and createdDate is unset. A federated storage provider that reconstructs the credential from the CredentialInput (as BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.getCredentials does, reading getCreatedDate() and getUserLabel()) will get a null/zero createdDate and null userLabel, so the stored federated credential loses the generatedAt metadata that the UI displays and that RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues expects. The OTP equivalent (createOTPCredential) similarly builds a minimal UserCredentialModel, but for OTP the secret is the only data. For recovery codes the createdDate/userLabel should be propagated (e.g. via UserCredentialModel.setUserLabel / credential data or by passing the full model) so federated storage round-trips the credential faithfully.

For a user whose recovery codes live in federated user storage, RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential returns the federated credential (from getFederatedCredentialsStream), and removeStoredCredentialById only removes credentials from the local Keycloak DB — it does not call the federated storage's disableCredentialType. The subsequent isConfiguredFor check (line 149) and the required-action re-trigger logic (lines 90-92) then operate on stale data: the federated credential still reports all codes used, but it is never deleted, so the credential lingers in the external storage indefinitely (a data-hygiene issue and potentially confusing state for the storage provider). The provider should hash the input (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode) and compare against hashed stored values, matching the local-storage validation semantics.
